name: RPC INC

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: That I am marking a trough to market and calling it a valuation. At $1.2bn of enterprise value against ~$263M of annualised adjusted EBITDA the name trades at 4.2x — for diversified oilfield services with ZERO debt and net cash, that is a normal-to-cheap trough multiple, not an expensive one, and my DCF only says 'rich' because it charges a full depreciation-level capex against trough EBITDA and then capitalises the remainder in perpetuity. That is precisely the AMR and LPG error in reverse: using a cyclical's worst earning power as the terminal base. The sequential evidence is a recovery, not a decline — margins 11.8% to 14.3% to 15.3% across three quarters, revenue rising, coiled tubing, nitrogen and snubbing each up double digits, and management describing 'current oil prices supporting a more favorable operating environment'. The working-capital drag is explicitly attributed to rising activity and to buying scarce components, which is what a company does on the way UP. And a debt-free survivor in a consolidating, oversupplied industry has option value that no five-year DCF off trough cash flow can express. On that reading the right base is mid-cycle $130-150M, which is roughly where the engine already sits, and the answer is the engine's +39% rather than my -12%.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Q4 2026 and the 2027 capital-expenditure guide, which the prior pass also nominated and which remain the right tests. Specifically: Q4 free cash flow above ~$50M would show the receivable and inventory build reversing and put the full-year base nearer $100M; 2027 capex guided below $130M, i.e. clearly beneath the ~$170M of depreciation, would prove that some of 2026's spend was growth rather than sustaining and that my whole-capex charge is too harsh; and a fourth consecutive quarter of adjusted EBITDA expansion (above ~$75M) would make the 2026 ramp a trend rather than three quarters. The cleanest single tell remains management's own: any announcement that RPC is reactivating frac fleets, which it has said it will not do at current pricing.
devils_advocate.already_visible: The evidence that is visible splits, which is why this is medium and not high conviction — but it splits unevenly, and the heavier half runs against the bull. For the bull: the margin ramp is real, monotonic and management-corroborated, and the balance sheet is genuinely unencumbered. Against it: the free-cash-flow test the last red team itself set was failed by a factor of fifty, and failed for the third consecutive period; capex sits BELOW depreciation, which removes the 'it is all growth spend' defence that would otherwise rescue the base; and the one acquisition that created the apparent growth has been impaired by $74.5M on management's own discounted-cash-flow forecast, which is the company telling me its own forward view of that asset fell short. I also cannot honestly treat 4.2x EV/EBITDA as evidence of cheapness when EBITDA converts to nothing — a multiple that ignores a capital intensity equal to 60% of EBITDA is the flattering frame, not the neutral one.
devils_advocate.unresolved: Whether 2026 is the cycle bottom. That is the whole question and I cannot settle it: at trough earning power the name is rich and at mid-cycle it is cheap, and the honest statement is that the price sits between those two. I also still do not have a disclosed maintenance-versus-growth capex split — I have inferred that essentially all of it is sustaining from capex being below depreciation, which is a strong inference but not the disclosure, and the 10-Q confirms the split exists internally ('the CODM assesses... growth and maintenance capital expenditures') without publishing it. And I could not correct the discount rate in the record, which matters more here than the base.

what_changed: The Q3 10-Q and earnings release were filed 2026-10-29, the day before this pass, and between them they answer both observables the previous devil's advocate (2026-09-03) nominated — and both answers go against the cheap case. (1) THE NOMINATED FREE-CASH-FLOW TEST FAILED. The prior pass wrote that the trough thesis required 'H2 2026 free cash flow above roughly $60M, with the working capital build reversing.' Nine-month free cash flow is $5.0M (CFO $115,732k less capex $110,727k), so third-quarter free cash flow was about $1.2M against the $3.8M reported at the half year. Not $60M — essentially nothing, for a third consecutive period. The release attributes the drag to 'higher accounts receivable resulting from increased customer activity and timing of collections, and strategic inventory purchases including key components in short supply', so part of it is genuine timing. (2) THE MAINTENANCE-VERSUS-GROWTH CAPEX SPLIT IS NOW EFFECTIVELY SETTLED, from the other direction. The prior pass left this open — 'if maintenance is $110M the business generates real cash at trough; if it is $160M it does not' — because management gives one combined number. The 10-Q still gives no split, but D&A of $42.7M a quarter (~$170M a year) exceeds annualised capex of ~$148M, so the company is not out-spending its own depreciation and there is no material growth-capex add-back available. The AROC pairing rule therefore does not rescue this base. (3) NEW AND DECISIVE ON THE BASELINE: a $74.5M non-cash impairment of Pintail ($58.3M of intangibles, $16.2M of PP&E), measured at 2026-08-31, because 'estimated undiscounted cash flows were less than the carrying amount of the asset group'. The prior pass's first key risk was that the +22.1% five-year revenue CAGR baseline was 'largely the Pintail Completions purchase' rather than mispricing; the write-down is the company confirming that in its own accounts. Net loss of $41.9M for the quarter. (4) Genuinely in the other direction, and the bull's best evidence: adjusted EBITDA has ramped monotonically through 2026 — $53.5M in Q1 (11.8% margin), $66.0M in Q2 (14.3%), $71.5M in Q3 (15.3%) — with revenue up 1% sequentially to $467.7M, double-digit sequential growth in coiled tubing, nitrogen and snubbing, and the $0.04 quarterly dividend maintained.
consensus_case: RPC is a debt-free, net-cash diversified oilfield services company in a structurally oversupplied US onshore market, and at $6.38 the market is paying roughly 4.2x enterprise value to annualised adjusted EBITDA for a business that cannot convert that EBITDA into free cash flow. The reason is capital intensity, and it is visible in two adjacent numbers: depreciation and amortisation ran $42.7M in the third quarter alone, about $170M a year, against capital expenditure of $110.7M for nine months, about $148M a year. Capex is therefore BELOW depreciation — this is sustaining spend, not a growth build — and nine-month free cash flow on the company's own definition was $5.0 million against $21.7M a year earlier. Three consecutive reporting periods have now produced free cash flow near zero. On top of that the market has just been handed management's own written admission that the acquisition which drove the apparent growth was a mistake: a $74.5M non-cash impairment of the Pintail wireline asset group, booked in the third quarter for 'persistent pricing weakness, lower activity and cost pressure'. Management has also said it will not reactivate frac fleets at current pricing. A market asking for roughly flat-to-modestly-positive real cash flow growth off genuine current earning power is not being pessimistic about any of that; it is being approximately right.
base_case_rationale: I underwrite zero real FCFF growth over five years off an overridden base of $78M rather than the engine's $132.3M, and the override is the substance of this pass. The engine's base is the mean of free cash flow of $52.9M, $129.5M and $213.8M (newest first) — a declining series whose oldest year is the 2022-23 post-COVID activity spike — and the business is not earning it. Built from current economics instead: full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA annualises to about $263M (nine months actual $191.0M plus a fourth quarter near the third's $71.5M); sustaining capital expenditure is between the $148M actually being spent and the $170M of depreciation, and since capex sits below D&A I take that whole range as sustaining; taxing the difference at 25% gives $70M at the D&A charge and $86M at the cash-capex charge, so $78M is the midpoint. On the growth rate, zero is the honest number and I keep the prior pass's figure for the same reasons plus one new one: US pressure pumping remains structurally oversupplied, management will not reactivate fleets at current pricing, inflation in labour, trucking and fuel is eating the activity recovery, and the wireline business has just been written down for persistent price weakness — against which the 2026 margin ramp and a debt-free balance sheet with net cash argue for eventual mid-cycle normalisation. Those roughly offset at zero. I differ from the naive +22.1% baseline because that figure is not a growth rate at all: it is five years of revenue CAGR largely created by buying Pintail for about $245M in April 2025, and applying acquired revenue growth to per-share free cash flow is the roll-up error from the standing lessons.
key_risks: Nine-month free cash flow of $5.0M against an engine base of $132.3M — the base is a three-year mean the business is not earning, and capex below depreciation removes the growth-capex defence
